reason: I ignored the numeric labels and block order and compared the same atom framework across conformers. The common, unavoidable aziridine ring strain is treated as approximately constant, so the discriminating terms are: (1) whether the alcohol O15-H16 can fold toward the tertiary aziridine N7 to give an intramolecular O-H···N hydrogen bond; (2) whether close O/N proximity is instead nonproductive because the O-H vector points away; and (3) gross steric placement of the n-propyl terminus C1 relative to the aziridine N/C8/C9 and the CH2OH group. I used approximate O15···N7, H16···N7 and O-H···N angle as the main metric: productive-looking contacts cluster around O···N 2.72-2.80 A and H···N 2.17-2.30 A with angles near 112-115 deg; weaker/borderline contacts have H···N about 2.34-2.36 A and angles near 110 deg; several conformers have O···N near 2.9 A but H···N 2.5-2.64 A and angles near 100 deg, which I count as nonproductive close contacts rather than hydrogen bonds; another set has O···N about 3.68 A and is simply non-hydrogen-bonded/extended. The best hydrogen-bond geometries appear for 19, 17, 20, 8, 30 and 23, with 19 shortest H···N and 17/20 essentially tied. A borderline H-bond group follows: 5, 12, 22, 15, 4, then weaker 27, 21, 13. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded extended set, I favored larger C1-to-N/C1-to-O separations and less methyl/aziridine crowding: 2, 18, 26, 29, 24, 14, 9 look comparatively open, while 10 has the terminal methyl much closer to N/aziridine and is penalized. The lowest group contains compact conformers where O and N are close but the OH hydrogen is oriented away, giving poor angles and likely O/N lone-pair or steric repulsion: 1, 25, 6, 3, 16, 11, 7, 28, with 7 and 28 the least convincing. Uncertainty is high within tiers because these are single-point geometries without energies; small changes in the O-H···N angle or aziridine rotation could swap neighbors, especially 17/20, 22/15/4, 27/21/13, and several of the extended conformers.

The molecule is CH3-CH2-NH-CH(CN)-C(=O)-NH2 (C5H9N3O, 18 atoms). Conformational energy is governed mainly by (i) possible intramolecular H-bonds, (ii) gauche/anti arrangement of the ethyl group on N3 relative to the -CN and -CONH2 substituents on the stereogenic alpha-carbon C5, and (iii) dipole alignment of the C=O and C≡N groups. Two H-bond motifs are plausible: a C5-type N3-H···O10=C contact (5-membered pseudocycle N3-C5-C9-O10, stabilizing when N3···O10 ≈ 2.8–3.1 Å and H4 points at O10), and an N11-H···N3 contact (amide NH2 donating to the secondary amine lone pair, N11···N3 ≈ 2.9–3.2 Å). The nitrile N7 is only a weak acceptor and a N3-H···N7 contact would be a strained ~4-membered ring, so I did not credit it. Steric penalties arise when the methyl C1 folds back toward the carbonyl O10 or nitrile (short C1···O10 / C1···N7 contacts) or when the ethyl is gauche to both the CN and CONH2 groups. Eclipsing along C2-N3 and C5-C9 also raises energy. Scanning the coordinates: several conformers (e.g. 16, 18, 27, 30, 5, 13) show an extended ethyl with N3-H roughly oriented toward the carbonyl O (short N3···O10) and the C=O/C≡N dipoles opposed, which I scored most stable. A middle group (6, 21, 15, 12, 3, 24, 7, 4, 17, 9) has either a weaker/longer H-bond, a single gauche ethyl interaction, or partial dipole alignment. Conformers where the amide NH2 instead closes toward N3 while the ethyl is folded (e.g. 20 shows a short N11···N3/H12···N3 contact but a tucked methyl), and structures with the methyl C1 pressed near O10/N7 or with nearly eclipsed C5-C9/C2-N3 bonds (8, 11, 14, 22, 23, 26, 28, 10, 19, 25, 2, 29, 1 in various degrees) were placed lower. The differences among many of these are small (a few kJ/mol) and, without electronic energies, the middle of the ordering is genuinely uncertain; I treated apparent heavy-atom contacts <~2.8 Å (H···H <~2.3 Å) as destabilizing and clean 5-ring N-H···O geometry as stabilizing. The order below is therefore a best-effort geometric estimate, with the largest confidence at the extremes and the least confidence in ranks ~8–24.

The connectivity is the same alanine-ethyl-ester-like framework: CH3CH2O-C(=O)-CH(NH2)-CH3. I ignored block order and numeric labels and compared invariant geometry: N···O=C distance and N-H···O alignment for a possible 5-membered intramolecular H-bond, N···O(ester) contacts for the weaker alternative H-bond, terminal ethoxy CH3 versus carbonyl O distance as a cis/trans ester-steric diagnostic, and alanine CH3 versus carbonyl O distance as an eclipsing/steric penalty. The clearest stabilizing motif is N-H···O=C with N···O about 2.78 A and one H···O about 2.35 A; this occurs in 1, 7, 8, 14, 15, 16. Among these, 16, 1, 7, 14 keep the ethoxy terminus away from the carbonyl O and have the largest methyl/methyl separations, so I place them first; 8 and especially 15 have the ethoxy CH3 much closer to the carbonyl O, consistent with a more cis/eclipsed ester arrangement, so they drop despite the good H-bond. A second set, 2, 5, 11, 18, 28, 29, has N near the carbonyl O but the N-H vectors are less well aligned, so the interaction is weaker/more bent; the trans-ethoxy members 5, 11, 29, 18 are favored over the more cis 28 and 2. Conformers 6, 10, 24, 26 lack the carbonyl H-bond but show the best N-H···O(ester) geometries and relatively relieved alanine-CH3/carbonyl-O contact; 26 and 24 are best because the ethoxy group is also anti, while 6 and 10 are more cis. The large middle group 3, 4, 12, 13, 19, 20, 21, 25, 27, 30, 9, 23 has only weaker ester-O contacts and/or short alanine-CH3···O=C distances around 3.03-3.10 A, with cis-ethoxy examples 23, 30, 9 penalized further; ordering within this band is uncertain. Finally 17 and 22 show the shortest alanine-CH3···O=C contacts, about 2.80 A, a clear steric/eclipsing penalty that outweighs their weak ester-O approach; 17 is placed last because it also has the most cis ethoxy/carbonyl relationship and the weaker N···O(ester) contact.

The molecule is CH3-C≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3 (C7H12O2): a rigid, linear methyl-alkyne 'rod' (C1-C2≡C3-C4) linked through an ether O (O5) to a flexible -CH2-CH(OH)-CH3 tail (C6-C7-O8-C10). The dominant conformational discriminator is whether the secondary alcohol O8-H9 can close a 5-membered pseudoring (O5···H9-O8-C7-C6-O5) and donate an intramolecular H-bond to the ether oxygen O5. I therefore measured O5···O8, H9···O5 and the O8-H9···O5 angle for every conformer. A genuine H-bond requires O5···O8 ≈ 2.7-2.8 Å AND H9···O5 ≈ 2.2-2.35 Å with the H pointed toward O5. Thirteen conformers satisfy this (5,9,12,13,16,17,18,21,24,27,28,29,30); the rest have either O···O ≈ 3.1-3.7 Å (no ring closure) or O···O ≈ 2.78 Å but the OH rotated away so H9···O5 ≈ 2.78-2.79 Å (a 'near-miss'). Within the H-bonded set, 13, 12 and 5 have the shortest H···O (~2.21 Å), near-ideal O···O (~2.77 Å) and the widest angle (~116°), i.e. the strongest, least-strained ring; 16 is equally short (O···O 2.74, H···O 2.21) but the ring is slightly compressed. 18, 29, 28, 17 form the next tier (O···O ~2.77-2.78, H···O ~2.28-2.30, angle ~110°). 30 is a bit loose (O···O 2.81) though reasonably angled; 27, 24, 21 and 9 have the longest H···O (~2.33-2.34) and most acute angles (~107-108°), i.e. the weakest H-bonds of the bonded group. Because the alkyne rod keeps the two methyl termini far apart in nearly all of these, methyl-methyl clash is minor and H-bond quality is the ranking criterion; residual uncertainty within this 13-member block is moderate. The non-H-bonded conformers split into three geometric classes: (a) extended/anti O5-C6-C7-O8 with O···O ≈ 3.6-3.7 Å (1,2,8,10,14,19,20,23,26) — no H-bond but also no close O···O contact, the least-bad of the non-bonded; (b) intermediate gauche O···O ≈ 3.1-3.26 Å (4,6,11,15,25) where the oxygens are brought into the same region (lone-pair/dipole repulsion) without an H-bond payoff; and (c) 'near-miss' geometries 3, 7, 22 where O···O is already ~2.78 Å (the two oxygens are at van-der-Waals contact, lone pairs facing) yet the OH hydrogen points away (H9···O5 ≈ 2.78-2.79), giving an unfavorable close O···O contact with zero H-bond stabilization — these should be the least stable. Ordering within class (a) is the most uncertain since all are comparably extended and differ only in small torsional/eclipsing details of the ethyl tail; I spread 20,14,1,23,2,10,19,26,8 by eyeballing stagger vs. eclipsing about C6-C7 and C7-C10. Net: all 13 intramolecular-H-bond conformers outrank all non-bonded ones; the extended anti non-bonded sit in the middle; the close-but-unbonded O···O cases (3,7,22) are placed last. The main uncertainty is the fine ordering inside the 13 H-bonded structures (differences of a few tenths of an Å) and inside the extended class (a), where no strong geometric feature separates members.

The structures are conformers of the same vicinal diol containing a cyclopropane ring, so the main discriminators are the relative orientation of the two hydroxyl groups, their ability to form an intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond, and 1,4 contacts involving the isopropyl group, tertiary alcohol oxygen, and cyclopropyl ring. The cyclopropane C-C bonds remain near 1.49-1.53 A in all structures, and bond lengths otherwise look normal; ring strain is therefore not a useful discriminator. No conformer shows an obviously impossible heavy-atom overlap, so the ranking is dominated by conformational rather than bonding strain. I evaluated both O...O separations and the shorter donor-H...acceptor distances, together with the approximate O-H...O angle. Conformers 2, 11, and 1 have the clearest intramolecular hydrogen bonds: conformer 2 has O...O about 2.66 A, H...O about 2.03 A, and an angle near 121 degrees; 11 and 1 are slightly longer or less linear, with H...O around 2.14-2.15 A and angles near 119-120 degrees. These three are placed first. Conformers 17 and 15 form the next-best interactions: 17 has the shorter H...O contact, about 2.19 A, while 15 has the better angle, about 115 degrees, but a longer 2.32 A contact. Conformers 26, 14, 3, 24, 9, and 29 have progressively weaker, bent contacts, roughly 2.30-2.51 A and 106-109 degrees. Their ordering is uncertain because shorter contact distance and better angular alignment sometimes trade against one another. The next group consists mainly of anti or extended hydroxyl arrangements with O...O distances around 3.54-3.68 A. They lack a significant hydrogen bond but avoid oxygen-oxygen compression. Within this group I favored conformers that also keep the isopropyl group away from the tertiary alcohol oxygen and the cyclopropyl ring: 7, 20, and 8 are relatively uncompromised, whereas 30, 5, 6, 22, and 16 show moderate C...O contacts near 2.9-3.0 A. Conformer 4 has an especially short methyl-to-hydroxyl-oxygen contact near 2.86 A, and 12 has a particularly compressed isopropyl-to-oxygen contact near 2.7 A, lowering them despite their extended O...O separations. Conformer 21 has a weak bent H...O contact, but its approximately 2.87 A isopropyl-to-oxygen contact offsets much of that benefit, so it is placed among the poorer extended structures. The last structures have close oxygens without useful hydrogen-bond alignment or an additional steric penalty. Conformer 10 is the least problematic of these; 13 has a short 2.74 A O...O separation and only a highly bent side-on H...O contact; 27 has an approximately 72 degree O-H...O angle, effectively removing hydrogen-bond stabilization; and 19 combines no useful hydrogen bond with a very short isopropyl-to-oxygen contact near 2.77 A, making it the least stable. The largest uncertainties are within the weakly hydrogen-bonded tier and among the extended conformers, where differences are probably on the order of ordinary torsional and dispersion contributions rather than qualitative structural changes.

Using the common atom ordering, the molecule consists of a central methine carbon bearing an ethyl group, an aziridinyl nitrogen, and a methoxymethyl group. The nitrogen and oxygen are both acceptors only; there are no N-H or O-H donors, so none of the conformers gains a conventional intramolecular hydrogen bond. I therefore compared staggered-versus-gauche relationships and short nonbonded contacts. The principal descriptors were: terminal ethyl carbon C1 to aziridine N6 and to methoxymethyl carbon C13; the methoxy torsion, where C5...C15 near 3.67-3.70 Å is anti and about 3.1 Å is gauche; the N6...O14 separation, where about 3.6-3.8 Å is relatively unhindered and 2.9-3.1 Å is crowded or at least dipole-unfavorable; and contacts of either terminal methyl group with the aziridine ring carbons, especially those near 3.3 Å. Conformer 16 is the cleanest overall: the ethyl group is anti to the aziridine nitrogen, the methoxy chain is extended, N...O is about 3.61 Å, and both terminal groups are more than roughly 4.4 Å from the ring carbons. Conformers 13 and 21 also have extended methoxy chains, anti-like N...O arrangements, and the aziridine ring rotated away from the ethyl group; their ethyl terminus is gauche to nitrogen, but the bulky ring carbons avoid it. Conformer 15 is similarly extended but has a shorter N...O contact near 3.03 Å. Conformers 22, 26, 10, and 23 keep the ethyl group away from the aziridine and have N...O near 3.68 Å, but their methoxy termini are gauche to the central carbon; their order follows the progressively shorter terminal-methyl separation, about 3.92, 3.88, 3.84, and 3.78 Å. Conformers 30, 2, and 6 have favorable extended methoxy and N...O geometry, but 30 has the ethyl terminus gauche to both central substituents, while 2 and 6 each place a terminal methyl about 3.3 Å from an aziridine carbon. Conformers 7, 4, and 9 avoid severe ring contacts but combine a gauche methoxy group with N...O distances around 3.12-3.17 Å. Conformers 17, 29, and 8 are also extended but have progressively less favorable combinations of C1...N near 2.9 Å and N...O near 3.10, 3.11, and 3.02 Å. Conformers 19, 18, and especially 5 accumulate several moderate gauche contacts rather than one decisive clash. The lower group contains clearer crowding: 25, 28, and 1 have methyl-aziridine contacts near 3.29-3.31 Å together with N...O contacts around 3.04-3.11 Å; 11 has a roughly 3.35 Å ring contact plus a gauche methoxy chain; 14 and 27 have the ethyl terminus gauche to both bulky branches and a gauche ether chain, although without a very short ring contact. Conformers 3 and 12 place the methoxy methyl only about 3.35 and 3.33 Å from an aziridine carbon and also have very short N...O separations near 2.94 and 2.91 Å. Conformer 20 combines a doubly gauche ethyl arrangement, N...O near 3.02 Å, and an ether-methyl/ring contact near 3.43 Å. Conformer 24 is placed last because it combines the doubly gauche ethyl arrangement, a gauche methoxy chain, N...O near 3.05 Å, and the two terminal methyl groups at only about 3.54 Å, giving the broadest accumulation of steric strain. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because a short N...O distance could be partly offset by favorable dipole or stereoelectronic alignment, and the force-field treatment of tertiary-amine versus ether gauche penalties can interchange closely spaced structures.

All blocks share the same atom order and connectivity: a C7H16O2 acyclic diol, CH3-CH2-CH(OH)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH2-OH (O at index 9 = OH on C8; O at index 19 = terminal OH on C18), with stereocenters at C8 and C12 and methyl branches C1 (via C5) and C13. Because there are no energies, I scored each geometry mainly by (a) intramolecular O-H···O bond formation, using O9···O19 distance plus the donor-H···acceptor distance and approximate O-H···O linearity, (b) O···O lone-pair repulsion when the two oxygens are close (~2.8-3.0 A) but the hydroxyl H atoms point away (no H-bond), and (c) extended/anti vs folded/gauche arrangement of the two methyl groups and the C8-O9 / C18-O19 dipoles. Computing O9···O19 for every conformer gives a clear split: (i) Strong, near-linear intramolecular H-bonds (O···O ~2.73-2.82 A, H···O ~1.82-1.92 A, donor angle ~150-158 deg): 1, 3, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 16, 18, 19, 22, 24, 27, 30. Within these I ranked shorter/more-linear H-bonds and less methyl syn-clash higher: 1, 12, 16, 27, 24, 30 are best (H···O ~1.82-1.86, ~154-158 deg); 13, 18, 7, 8, 22, 3 next (slightly longer or ~150 deg); 19 and 10 are the weakest of this H-bonded set (H···O ~1.91-1.92). (ii) Weaker/longer or more bent H-bonds (H···O ~1.95-1.98, angle ~145-152 deg, or O···O ~2.84-2.87): 9, 15, 23, 17 - still net stabilizing but less than group (i). (iii) Extended conformers with O···O ~3.9-5.2 A (2, 4, 11, 14, 20, 21, 26, 29): no H-bond but also no O···O repulsion; the fully extended, dipole-separated ones (20, 21, 2, 29) are the cleanest of the non-H-bonded set and sit just below the weak-H-bond group, while 4, 11, 14, 26 (O···O ~3.6-3.9, more gauche/folded without bonding) are a bit lower. (iv) Least favorable: oxygens held at ~2.88-2.99 A yet the OH protons are not directed at the other oxygen (H···O ~2.3-2.5, donor angle far from linear, e.g. conformer 28 has O-H···O angle ~49 deg), so close O···O lone-pair/steric repulsion is paid without an H-bond gain: 28, 6, 5, 25, with 25 and 5 looking most cramped/misaligned. Uncertainty: hand-estimated distances/angles cannot resolve subtleties such as exact methyl-methyl gauche penalties or small dipole differences, so the ordering within the large H-bonded block (especially positions ~5-14) and within the extended block is only approximate; the robust conclusions are that the near-linear H-bonded set is most stable, extended/anti non-bonded forms are intermediate, and close-but-nonbonded O···O geometries are least stable.

I treated the block order and numeric labels as arbitrary and compared only geometry. The connectivity appears constant: a methyl ketone attached through CH2 to a strained cyclopropane bearing two OH groups, so cyclopropane ring strain is approximately common to all conformers and the main discriminators are intramolecular OH...O=C hydrogen bonds, OH/OH orientation, carbonyl dipole alignment, and close nonbonded contacts. I estimated donor-H...acceptor distances from the coordinates: conformers 3, 21, 9, 10, 22, 18, 12, 24, 20, 25 and 7 show the clearest OH...O=C contacts, with H...O roughly 1.9-2.2 A and O...O near 2.8-2.85 A; I ranked 3/21/9/10 highest because the donor H is closest to the carbonyl O while keeping a reasonable O-H...O angle, and placed 7 last among this set because its H...O contact is visibly longer. Conformers 4, 27, 17, 30, 14 and 11 have only moderate or geometrically poorer contacts, about 2.3-2.8 A H...O or longer O...O separations, so they follow. The remaining structures are more open: the two OH groups are typically ~3.6-3.8 A apart, not close enough for a strong vicinal-diol hydrogen bond, and neither OH hydrogen is well directed at the carbonyl oxygen; among them I used compactness, approximate carbonyl/OH dipole opposition, and absence of obvious methyl/ring crowding only as weak tie-breakers. The middle and especially the no-clear-H-bond group are uncertain because these are coordinate-only estimates, small rotations of OH hydrogens can change H...O distances, and no entropic or electronic-energy data are available.

The common connectivity is CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CHO)-COCH3: one hydroxyl donor, an aldehyde carbonyl acceptor, and a ketone carbonyl acceptor. Bond lengths and angles are ordinary throughout, so relative stability is controlled mainly by the OH...O=C geometry, staggering about the carbinol-central C-C bond, carbonyl-dipole orientation, and methyl/carbonyl crowding. I first compared the hydroxyl H with both carbonyl oxygens. Clear ketone-side hydrogen bonds occur in 19, 17, 14, 24, 2, and 28; clear aldehyde-side bonds occur in 8, 18, 12, 11, 3, and 23. Conformer 19 has the best contact, H...O approximately 1.93 A and O-H...O approximately 136 degrees, with a staggered backbone and opposed carbonyl dipoles. Conformer 8 has a short aldehyde-side bond, about 2.00 A and 132 degrees, and nearly antiparallel carbonyls. Conformers 17 and 14 have strong ketone-side contacts of roughly 2.0-2.1 A; 17 gains from better carbonyl opposition, while 14 has essentially ideal staggering. Conformer 18 also has a strong aldehyde-side bond, but its two methyl carbons are relatively close, about 3.4 A. Conformers 28, 12, 24, and 11 form somewhat longer or less linear bonds. Conformer 24 has the shorter contact and ideal staggering, but less favorable carbonyl-dipole alignment than 11. Conformers 3 and 23 are nearly degenerate, each with H...O around 2.23-2.24 A and an angle near 124 degrees; 3 is marginally better geometrically. Conformer 2 has a real ketone-side bond, but its carbonyl dipoles are more parallel and the backbone has a near-eclipsed methyl/H relationship, so it is the weakest of the hydrogen-bonded group. Among structures without a viable OH...O bond, 22 and 29 are the most attractive: they are well staggered and have opposed carbonyl dipoles. Conformers 21, 4, 25, and 1 also oppose the carbonyl dipoles but show modest torsional imperfections. Conformers 26, 13, 9, 6, 30, and 16 form the next broad cluster, trading progressively weaker dipole opposition against generally good staggering. Conformers 27 and 5 have less favorable carbonyl orientations and some torsional mismatch. Near the bottom, 15 has partially aligned carbonyls and imperfect staggering; 7 has the carbonyl oxygens relatively close with aligned dipoles despite good backbone staggering; 20 has several substantially nonideal torsions even though its carbonyls are opposed; and 10 combines aligned carbonyl dipoles, a close carbonyl-O/OH-O approach without hydrogen bonding, and a particularly poor near-eclipsed C/H relationship. The largest uncertainties are the order of 8, 17, and 14; the nearly tied pair 3/23; and the boundary between the weakest hydrogen-bonded conformer 2 and the best non-hydrogen-bonded conformer 22.

The framework is the same in all 30 blocks: an NH-pyrrole ring bearing an ethyl group and a hydroxymethyl group. I treated ring strain as essentially constant because the five-membered ring stays near planar; the discriminating terms are therefore (1) N-H···O intramolecular H-bonding from the pyrrole N-H to the CH2OH oxygen, (2) ethyl rotation that can put the terminal methyl near the N-H/ring edge, and (3) cross-substituent crowding between ethyl and hydroxymethyl groups. Estimating key contacts from the coordinates: conformers 23 and 27 uniquely have short N···O distances around 2.7 Å with H(N)···O around 2.4 Å, consistent with a real, though not perfectly linear, intramolecular N-H···O bond; both still have the ethyl in the closer rotamer, so the H-bond must compensate. Conformer 10 is the clear outlier at the unfavorable end: the ethyl methyl is much closer to the pyrrole N/N-H region than in the others, indicating a methyl/N-H steric clash despite an otherwise moderate O position. Several conformers fall into an ethyl-relaxed group with methyl-to-N contacts around 3.75-4.22 Å (notably 18, 4, 8, 5, 20, 15, 26, 14, 1, 11, 16); among these I favored shorter/less awkward O···N approaches and larger ethyl-to-hydroxymethyl separation, so 18/4/8 rank highest, followed by 5/20/15/26 and then the more O-distant 14/1/11/16. The ethyl-closer rotamers without a strong H-bond were penalized; within that set I ordered mainly by increasing O···N separation and apparent N-H···O plausibility: 3 and 25 have moderate O approach, 21/29/24/9/7/28/30/17/12/19/13 progressively weaker, and 2/22/6 are both ethyl-close and O-distant. Differences in the middle are subtle and probably within a few kcal/mol; the most robust features are 23/27 at the top and 10 at the bottom.

1) The connectivity is a tertiary alcohol bearing methyl, CH2CHO, and CH2C≡CH substituents. Bond lengths are normal in every structure, and there is no covalent ring; therefore, conventional ring strain is not a discriminator. The main geometric factors are internal hydrogen bonding, weak OH···alkyne contacts, folded substituent contacts, and H···H crowding. Most central tetrahedral arrangements are approximately staggered, so eclipsing differences are secondary. 2) The strongest stabilization is a five-membered O-H···O=C pseudocycle. Six conformers have short alcohol-oxygen/carbonyl-oxygen separations of about 2.76–2.85 Å. Approximate H···O distances and O-H···O angles are: 30: 1.94 Å, 139°; 9: 2.07 Å, 131°; 2: 2.08 Å, 131°; 18: 2.11 Å, 129°; 26: 2.12 Å, 127°; and 4: 2.14 Å, 127°. Conformer 30 has the clearly best hydrogen bond; although its aldehyde and alkyne ends are folded toward one another, the closest H···H contact remains above 3 Å, so this is not a severe clash. Conformer 2 combines a strong hydrogen bond with a comparatively open periphery and is placed ahead of 9. Conformers 9, 18, and 26 have somewhat closer methyl/formyl-side contacts but no severe H···H overlap. Conformer 4 is open but has the longest hydrogen bond; 26 and 4 are particularly close and could reasonably be interchanged. 3) A second group has the OH directed toward the alkyne π system rather than the carbonyl. Approximate H-to-alkyne-midpoint distances are 19: 2.51 Å, 7: 2.55 Å, 17: 2.57 Å, 11 and 29: about 2.60–2.61 Å, 15: 2.63 Å, 14, 23, 8, and 3: about 2.65 Å, 6: 2.67 Å, and 21 and 5: about 2.71 Å, with donor angles mostly near 115–122°. These contacts are weaker and more bent than the carbonyl hydrogen bonds, so all are ranked below the first six. Within this group, 19 and 7 have the best π-contact geometry; 11 also has a short methyl-C-H···O contact around 2.43 Å, while 14 and 8 are less crowded overall. Conformers 19, 17, 29, and 3 incur mild formyl/methyl H···H contacts of roughly 2.5–2.7 Å. Conformer 23 has a good OH···π distance but a much shorter formyl-H/methyl-H contact near 2.26 Å, so it is dropped below the cleaner members of this tier. 4) The remaining conformers lack a short, directional OH···O or OH···π interaction. Conformers 12, 25, and 13 are relatively open; 12 and 25 also orient the hydroxyl at least somewhat toward the carbonyl, whereas 13 points it away. Conformer 28 is next because its termini are well separated despite a closer methyl/formyl side. Conformer 10 is compact but avoids a very short H···H contact. Conformer 27 gains some compensation from an approximately 2.25 Å methyl-C-H···O contact. Conformers 24, 16, and 22 direct the hydroxyl proton away from the carbonyl oxygen; 22 additionally folds the carbonyl group close to the alkyne. The least stable pair is 20 and 1: both are compact, lack an internal hydrogen bond, and contain severe formyl-H/methyl-H contacts of about 2.30 and 2.25 Å, respectively. Conformer 1 also has the less favorable alcohol/carbonyl dipole orientation and is therefore placed last. The largest uncertainty is within the OH···π tier and among conformers 24, 16, and 22, where several separations are probably sub-kcal to about 1 kcal/mol; the six carbonyl-hydrogen-bonded conformers at the top and 20/1 at the bottom are the most robust features.

I treated the invariant atom order as a 2,5-disubstituted tetrahydrofuran-like scaffold: O9 is the ring ether oxygen, C1 is the methyl substituent on one ring stereocenter, C10 is the other substituted ring carbon, and C11-C13-O15-H16 is the hydroxyethyl side chain. The dominant discriminator is therefore whether the terminal OH can donate an intramolecular H bond to the ring ether oxygen: conformers 11, 24, 26, 28, 29 and 8 have short O9...O15 separations (~2.77-2.80 A) and, more importantly, H16...O9 distances near ~2.0 A, so they form a folded five/six-membered pseudoring H bond. Among these, 26 and 29 look best: H16...O9 is shortest and the O9...O15 distance is in the normal H-bond range; 8 and 24 are also very good, with 8 having slightly less substituent crowding but a marginally longer H...O contact; 11 has a strong H bond but the shortest methyl/side-chain separation in the set, so I penalize it for cis-like 1,2 crowding; 28 is clearly H-bonded but its H16...O9 contact is the longest of the strong set. The remaining conformers lack a geometrically credible OH...O(ring) bond: either O9...O15 is >4 A, or the hydroxyl H points away even when the oxygens are moderately close. Within the non-H-bonded group I favored more extended/anti side chains and larger C1...C11 separations (roughly 3.05-3.08 A) over compact but non-H-bonded arrangements. Thus 20, 10, 27, 21, 4 and 30 are relatively benign extended structures; 14, 5, 23, 9, 25, 6, 12, 7, 15 and 19 are intermediate, with growing gauche/eclipsing or dipole penalties. The worst structures are compact yet not H-bonded: 18 has O9...O15 around 3.15 A but H16 is not directed at O9, implying oxygen lone-pair/dipole repulsion rather than stabilization; 3 is similar but weaker; 1 and 2 are folded with no H-bond payoff and relatively short methyl/side-chain contacts; 13, 16, 17 and 22 sit just above that repulsive compact class. The ordering inside the non-H-bonded middle is uncertain because ring-envelope strain and torsional eclipsing cannot be quantified exactly from coordinates alone, but the H-bonded sextet at the top and the compact non-H-bonded structures at the bottom are the most robust conclusions.

I treated the connectivity as CH3-C*(CHO)-CH2-O-CH=NH: an aldehyde acceptor at one end, an imidate/formimidate N-H at the other, and rotors mainly about C*-CHO, C*-CH2, CH2-O and O-C=N. I first looked for a stabilizing N-H···O=C contact: none of the 30 gives a clean short H15···O7 (~1.8-2.2 A) with N···O ~2.8-3.1 A and a pointing N-H. Several compact folds (20, 29, 30, 6) have N14···O7 ~2.6-2.7 A, but H15 is farther from O7 than N14 is, so the N-H points away; this brings two negative/lone-pair centers close rather than making a good H-bond, so I penalized rather than rewarded those folds. The largest repeated geometric signal is aldehyde rotation: carbonyl O7 syn/eclipsing to the methyl C1 gives C1···O7 ~2.8 A and was penalized (notably 1,2,3,4,10,13,16,19,20,21,23,25,27,28), whereas O7 anti to methyl gives ~3.3-3.7 A (5,6,7,8,9,11,12,14,15,17,18,22,24,26,30). Next I favored staggered/extended C*-CH2-O-CH=NH arrangements with the ether O and imidate end not stacked against the methyl group (C1···O12 preferably >3.3 A) and with the polar C=O and C=N ends separated enough to avoid like-charge N···O contact. Thus 5, 7, 22, 11 and 12 combine anti aldehyde rotation, relatively extended chains and no close N···O; 17, 24, 8, 26, 9, 18, 14 and 15 are still good but have some ether-O/methyl syn character or slightly less ideal chain stagger. 6 and 30 have good aldehyde rotation but compact N···O approaches, so they fall to mid rank. Bad aldehyde rotors are lower, ordered by how extended/unclashed the imidate chain is; 20 and 29 are worst because a short N14···O7 contact coincides with an unfavorable aldehyde/methyl geometry and no actual N-H···O bond. Uncertainty is high within the middle because without energies I am inferring from sterics/dipoles only, and small torsional differences could swap adjacent entries.

I treated the atom order as fixed: a methyl-bearing cyclohexene ring (C5-C6=C7-C8-C9-C10) with a hydroxymethyl substituent at C9. Because there are no energies, I used geometry proxies: (1) separation between the methyl carbon C1 and hydroxymethyl carbon C13 as a measure of whether the two substituents are splayed into pseudo-equatorial, non-interacting positions or folded toward one another; (2) whether the OH vector points outward from the ring rather than back into C-H/H-H contacts; (3) preservation of a normal cyclohexene half-chair with the C6=C7 bond not strongly twisted; (4) avoidance of close nonbonded contacts involving the methyl group, the CH2OH group, and allylic ring hydrogens. Conformers 25, 23, 8, 18, 16 and 3 look the most extended: large C1...C13 separations and the OH generally directed away from the ring, consistent with both substituents occupying less hindered pseudo-equatorial environments. 27, 30, 26, 17, 19, 28, 1 and 29 are also extended but show slightly less ideal OH placement or a bit more folding around the allylic C5-C6=C7 region. 24, 14, 13, 21 and 5 are intermediate: substituents are far apart, but some OH/ring orientations look less clean. 11 and 2 are middling-to-poor because the substituent separation is smaller, implying more steric interaction even though the ring is not grossly distorted. The least stable set is 12, 10, 4, 20, 22, 15, 7, 6 and especially 9: these have smaller C1...C13 distances and/or the hydroxymethyl group turned back toward the ring/methyl side, giving more 1,3-diaxial-like and H-H crowding. The ordering among the middle conformers is uncertain because cyclohexene pseudorotation makes axial/equatorial penalties smaller than in cyclohexane and a weak O-H...pi interaction could stabilize a few geometries that look compact by the simple distance proxy.

I treated the common connectivity as a flexible chain with two intramolecular H-bond donors (amide N-H and alcohol O-H) and two main acceptors (formamide carbonyl O and alcohol O). The most stabilizing geometries are those that put a donor H about 1.8-2.2 A from an acceptor O with a plausible pseudo-ring and without obvious methyl/hydroxymethyl crowding. Several conformers show a clear N-H...O(alcohol) six-membered contact: 18, 28, 19, 14, 6, 8 and 7 have H12...O19 roughly 1.9-2.2 A; I ranked these highly, with 18/28/19 best because the N...O separation is near 2.8-2.9 A and the chain looks folded rather than eclipsed. A second group has O-H...O=C contacts: 2, 13, 20, 3, 9, 16 and 10 show H20...O10 around 1.8-2.1 A; carbonyl is a strong acceptor, but the closure is a larger loop, so I placed the best of these just after the cleanest N-H...O forms. Within that OH...O=C set, 2 and 13 look shortest/most favorable, while 20, 3, 9, 16 and 10 are close; 11, 1 and 15 have H...O proximity but longer O...O separations and/or poorer donor-H-acceptor alignment, so they are mid-ranked rather than top. Conformers 22, 27 and 4 have only weak/long N-H...O or OH...O approaches, and 12, 30, 29, 26, 23, 25, 21, 5, 24 and 17 look mostly extended with no convincing intramolecular H bond; their ordering is dominated by avoiding close nonbonded contacts, but differences are subtle and uncertain. I did not use the numeric labels or block order as stability cues. The main uncertainty is that without energies I cannot distinguish entropic/extended conformers from weakly H-bonded folded ones, and some apparent H...O distances may be misleading if the donor-H-acceptor angle is poor; therefore middle ranks, especially 11-27, should be viewed as approximate.

All 30 share identical connectivity, including a strained three-membered aziridine (N–CH2–CH) fused to a –CH(OH)–CH(CH3)–CH2OH backbone; that intrinsic ring strain is constant, so it does not separate conformers. Differentiation therefore comes from (i) intramolecular H-bonding among the two OH donors/acceptors and the aziridine N (good acceptor), judged by heavy-atom O···O/O···N/N···O distances (~2.75–2.9 Å = strong; 3.0–3.3 = marginal) and whether the O–H/N–H proton points at the acceptor, and (ii) steric clashes. I screened the O_a/O_b/N triangle plus donor H positions for each structure. No conformer shows a severe heavy-atom clash (minimum heteroatom separations are ≈2.76 Å), so H-bond count/quality dominates. Clear winners are geometries that fold so O_a–H···O_b and O_b/N–H form a cooperative pair: 30 (2.76/2.77 Å), 21 (2.78/2.78), 4 (2.82/2.78), 11 (2.80/2.78), 14 (verified O_a–H···O_b ≈2.04 Å and N–H···O_b ≈2.36 Å), 3, 23, 5 (extra marginal contact), 20, 1 and 26 — these have two short heteroatom contacts and rank highest, ordered by how short/linear the pair is. A middle band (13,12,16,7,9,29,8,24,22,18,17,10,28,27) has exactly one solid H-bond (~2.77–2.80 Å) sometimes with a marginal second contact; within it I favored the shorter primary contact and any near-threshold second contact. The least stable are extended conformers with at most one weak/marginal N···O contact and the OH groups pointed away (15,6 ≈3.03–3.04; 19 ≈3.10; 25 ≈3.14; 2 ≈3.19, essentially no intramolecular H-bond), so 2 and 25 sit at the bottom. Uncertainty is high: I used heavy-atom distances as a proxy (not full DFT), proton orientation was checked only for a subset, dispersion and solvation are ignored, and several pairs within each tier are within ~0.05 Å of each other, so adjacent swaps (especially inside the large middle band) are plausible.

Molecule identified from the fixed atom order: an imidate CH3-C(=NH)-O-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH (atom2 = imidate C; N3-H4 imine; O5 = imidate/ether O; C6-C9 = four-carbon tether; O10-H11 = terminal OH). The dominant stabilizing geometry is therefore an intramolecular H-bond that folds the tether back onto the imidate head. The best motif is terminal O10-H11 donating to the imidate ether O5, which closes a favorable pseudo six-membered ring (O5-C6-C7-C8-C9-O10). I screened d(O5...O10), d(H11...O5) and the O10-H11...O5 angle for all 30, and used d(N3...O10) for the less favorable 8-ring alternative, plus chain extension (larger O5...O10 = fewer gauche contacts) as a tie-breaker among non-H-bonded forms.

Strong 6-ring OH...O5 H-bonds (O...O ~2.8 A, H...O ~1.9 A, near-linear ~150 deg): 18 (2.80/1.87/154), 27 (2.80/1.90/149), 22 (2.80/1.91/149) are essentially tied at the top, with 18 marginally best (shortest H...O, most linear). 29 (2.92/2.02/149) is the next clear H-bonded case. Moderate, more bent 6-ring H-bonds: 3 (2.88/2.09/~136) and 4 (3.01/2.22/~136); both are stabilized but noticeably bent/longer, so they sit below the tight four. Near-miss/borderline folds where O5...O10 is short-ish but H11 is misdirected or the contact is too long (6 shows only a weak/long N...O ~3.18 with OH pointing away; 10 O...O 3.35 bent; 8 O...O 3.50 H away; 12 O...O 3.42 H away; 28 O...O 3.52 H away) get little net H-bond yet pay some fold strain, placing them just under 3/4 with order uncertain.

Among the clearly non-H-bonded conformers I favored more extended anti tethers (less gauche/eclipsing strain) over compact-but-nonbonding folds. Most extended/clean: 1 (O...O ~6.2), then 2, 9, 26, 5, 20, 30, 19 (all ~5.2). Progressively less extended or mildly folded without an H-bond payoff: 14, 17, 16, 11, 24, 23, 25. The worst are compact/curling geometries that incur close contacts and gauche strain yet form no H-bond: 21, 13, 15, and 7 (linear-looking but with an unfavorable imidate/tether disposition and no compensating bond), placed last. The top four and the bottom few are reasonably confident; the middle (roughly positions 7-27) is uncertain because extended anti chains trade a small loss of gauche strain against the absence of an intramolecular H-bond, and no energies are available.

The atom list is consistent with a nitrile–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–CH(cyclopropyl) framework: N≡C–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–CH–(CH2–CH2) with a rigid cyclopropane at the end. There are no N–H or O–H donors, so conventional intramolecular hydrogen bonding is not available; ranking therefore rests mainly on (1) staggered vs eclipsed rotors about C–C, C–O and O–C bonds, (2) keeping the polar nitrile/ether end away from the compact cyclopropyl end, and (3) avoiding folded geometries that bring CH2 groups or the cyclopropane C–H bonds into short H···H/C···H contact. I treated large end-to-end separation plus an anti, extended C3–O–C5–C6–C7 sequence as favorable, and hairpin turns that place the cyanomethoxy group back over C6/C7/cyclopropane as unfavorable. Conformers 25, 10, 7, 28, 15 and 9 look the most extended and least congested, with the nitrile end well separated from the cyclopropane and no obvious heteroatom/ring clash. Conformers 24, 4, 21, 22, 2 and 14 are also extended but show somewhat more gauche character around the ether linkage or cyclopropane attachment. The middle set (19, 17, 13, 12, 8, 30, 6, 29, 27) has one or more folded/gauche segments, possible eclipsing near C5–C6–C7, or closer approach of the ether oxygen to the cyclopropyl methylene groups, so they are placed lower. The least stable group is 20, 3, 5, 23, 18, 1, 11, 26 and especially 16: these are more compact, with shorter nitrile-to-cyclopropane distances and/or turns that bring C3/O/C5 back toward C6–C9, implying more gauche penalties and nonbonded H···H crowding. Differences within the middle are subtle because bond lengths and the cyclopropane ring are similar; uncertainty is highest for 17–27 and for 3/5/20/23, where a small torsional change could swap several positions.

I treated the connectivity as a seven-membered oxepene-like ring: C4=C5-C6-C8-C10-O11-C12-C4, with a hydroxymethyl substituent C3-O1H2 on the alkene carbon C4. First I looked for an intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond. In essentially every structure the alcohol O1 is far from the ring ether O11: most O1...O11 distances are about 4.1-4.9 A, and even the shorter cases are only around 3.6-3.7 A with the hydroxyl H not in a short, linear H...O contact. So no conformer gains a strong conventional intramolecular H bond; the ranking is therefore dominated by ring strain, alkene planarity, allylic C3/C12 crowding at C4, staggered versus eclipsed methylenes, transannular H...H proximity, and whether the two oxygen dipoles are separated rather than folded toward one another. I favored conformers that look extended/chair- or twist-chair-like around C6-C8-C10-O11-C12, keep the C4=C5 unit close to planar, put CH2OH pseudo-equatorial/away from the ring, and separate O1 from O11. I penalized compact folded rings, twisted alkene/allylic strain at C4, eclipsed methylene sequences, and the few structures where O1/O11 are comparatively close or the OH vector points back into the ring without a true H bond, which suggests dipole/lone-pair crowding rather than stabilization. The most stable group appears to be 23, 17, 6, 5 and 19: these have large O1...O11 separations, an exposed/anti hydroxymethyl group, and a reasonably staggered methylene chain. 18, 27, 21, 11 and 22 are similar but show somewhat more folding or less clean staggering. The middle group 10, 20, 15, 1, 12, 16, 24, 29, 30, 3 contains mixed ring puckers: no severe clash is obvious, but either the ring is more twisted, the CH2OH orientation is less favorable, or the alkene/allylic region looks more crowded. Conformers 14, 25, 26, 13 and 2 look increasingly compact or eclipsed, with less favorable transannular/allylic contacts. The least stable are assigned to 28, 4, 9, 8 and especially 7: these have the shortest O1...O11 separations and/or OH orientations directed back toward the ether oxygen/ring interior at non-hydrogen-bonding distances, implying unfavorable close polar contacts plus more folded methylene geometry. The uncertainty is significant because without torsional energies or explicit MM/QM values several middle-ring conformers could interchange; in particular a weak electrostatic attraction in 7/8/4 could stabilize them relative to my placement, while an extended structure could still be strained if its alkene is twisted.

Connectivity (same in all): a 6‑membered oxane/tetrahydropyran ring (ring O = atom 12) bearing a flexible ‑CH2‑CH2‑OH arm whose terminal OH is atom1(H atom2). The dominant stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O1–H2···O12 hydrogen bond when the arm folds back onto the ring oxygen; absent that, stability is governed by having the two oxygens far apart (low O···O lone‑pair repulsion/dipole, relaxed anti geometry) versus being folded into a close, non‑bonded O···O contact that is repulsive.

I computed O1···O12 and H2···O12 for each conformer. Only two show a genuine H‑bond: Conformer 14 (O···O ≈ 2.94 Å, H···O ≈ 2.00 Å, O–H···O ≈ 164°) and Conformer 9 (O···O ≈ 2.95 Å, H···O ≈ 2.06 Å, ≈161°). Both are clearly most stable; 14 is marginally shorter/more linear, so I place it first, but 9 and 14 are essentially interchangeable within uncertainty.

All other conformers lack this H‑bond (H2 points away from O12 and/or O···O is large). Among them I used O1···O12 as a proxy for relaxed‑extended (favorable) vs folded‑repulsive (unfavorable): large separations (~5.6–6.0 Å) imply an extended, low‑strain anti arrangement of the two C–O bonds and are favored (25≈5.99, 23≈5.98, 8≈5.94, 29≈5.89, 28≈5.85, 5≈5.80, 16≈5.71, 17≈5.70, 20≈5.68, 19≈5.66, 12≈5.63). Intermediate (~5.0–5.4) are next (13,6,30,4,10,7,26,11). The least stable are conformers that bring the two oxygens to ~3.85–4.45 Å without an H‑bond, giving O···O lone‑pair repulsion plus folding strain: 1(4.44),24(4.40),22(4.28),2(4.11),18(3.90),27(3.90),15(3.85); 15 has the shortest O···O with H2 farthest (≈4.53 Å), so it is the most repulsive and is ranked last, with 27 and 18 just above it.

Uncertainty: the 14/9 order could swap; the ordering within the large 'extended' block and within the 'folded‑repulsive' block is only approximate because ring‑pucker (chair vs twist‑boat) and local gauche penalties could reshuffle neighbors by a few positions.

The atom order implies the same C6H12O2 framework in every block: a strained four-carbon ring (atoms 5-7-10-13) bearing a 2-hydroxyethyl arm at C5 and an OH at C10. Bond lengths and the near-constant ring diagonals suggest the cyclobutane strain is broadly similar across the set, so the discriminating terms are intramolecular O-H...O bonding, folding/gauche strain in the O-C-C-C arm, and close O...O or O-H...H contacts. I first screened O1...O11 distances and H...O geometries: conformers 8, 3, 14 and 4 have O...O around 2.9 A with a short, nearly linear O-H...O contact, so they are clearly favored; 8 and 3 look the most linear/short, 14 is comparable, and 4 is slightly longer/weaker. Most other conformers have O...O >5 A and no donor-acceptor alignment, so they lose several kcal/mol of H-bond stabilization. Among those, I favored extended anti-like arms with the two OH groups well separated and few folded contacts: 6, 24, 11, 30, 22, 12 and 27, followed by 17 which is a little more folded but still avoids close O...O contact. Conformers 23, 29 and 5 are compact enough to bring the oxygens to roughly 4 A but without a real H bond, so they get only weak/ambiguous electrostatic benefit and some repulsion risk. The remaining structures are increasingly gauche/folded in the hydroxyethyl arm without compensating H-bonding; I ordered them by approximate O1...C5 extension and by whether the terminal OH is folded back toward the ring or merely points into empty space, putting the shortest/most folded non-H-bonded cases last. The middle and lower parts are uncertain because cyclobutane puckering, local dipole alignment and small H...H clashes are hard to separate visually.

I ignored the numeric labels and block order and compared only geometry. The connectivity appears to be an aldehyde at one end, a flexible methylene linker, a rigid alkyne-like C7-C8 segment, and a terminal strained aziridine ring bearing the N-H. I therefore scored three features: (1) possible N-H...O=C interaction using O1...H12/O1...N11 separation and approximate directionality; (2) preservation of a nearly linear C6-C7-C8-C9 alkyne axis and anti, non-eclipsed methylene torsions; (3) close nonbonded contacts from folding the carbonyl end back toward the aziridine. No conformer shows a short linear hydrogen bond: the closest approaches are Conformer 13 (O...H about 3.7 A, O...N about 4.5 A, bent but plausibly weakly attractive) and Conformer 28 (about 3.9/4.7 A), so I place those first but with low confidence. Conformer 9 also brings the ends together, but the N-H...O angle is much more bent and the carbonyl oxygen approaches the aziridine nitrogen/lone-pair region rather than cleanly meeting the N-H, so I treat it as less favorable and potentially more repulsive. The extended structures 29, 24, 12, 20, 27, 30, 3 and 16 keep the alkyne segment nearly collinear, avoid end-to-end contacts, and reduce methylene eclipsing; among them 29 is especially straight, while 24/12/20 are similarly extended with slightly different terminal aziridine orientations. Mid-ranked conformers such as 19, 14, 25, 8, 7, 17, 23, 6, 11 and 10 are mostly extended or mildly folded but show either less ideal carbonyl/methylene torsion alignment or less favorable aziridine orientation. Lower-ranked conformers 22, 1, 2, 26, 18, 4 and 5 are more kinked without a compensating short N-H...O contact, suggesting higher torsional/steric cost. Conformers 21, 15 and especially 9 are put near the bottom because compactness brings heteroatom termini into the same region with poor hydrogen-bond geometry and likely lone-pair/dipole mismatch rather than a stabilizing contact. The separation between many mid-list structures is small, and a real quantum or force-field energy could reorder several adjacent pairs, especially within the extended group.

I ignored the numeric labels and block order. The atom order is consistent, so the connectivity appears to contain a common four-membered oxetane-like ring (O17-C14-C6-C4) bearing a hydroxymethyl arm at C4 (C3-O1-H2) and a formylmethyl/aldehyde arm at C6 (C7-C8=O9-H10). Because the oxetane ring and stereochemistry are common, most ring strain cancels; the ranking is driven mainly by (1) whether the single OH donor makes a good intramolecular H-bond, (2) whether the carbonyl is folded into a non-H-bonded close O...O/steric contact, and (3) whether the two polar arms are extended enough to avoid H...H and O...O clashes. A clear O1-H2...O9 carbonyl H-bond is the strongest stabilizing motif: Conformer 22 has the best geometry (short H...O contact, nearly linear O-H...O), 5 is also strong with a short O...O distance, and 13 is similarly H-bonded but a little more folded/sterically crowded. The next tier donates to the weaker ring ether O17: 14, 21, 25, 15, 7, 8, 3 and 4 show O1...O17 around 2.7-2.8 A with H2...O17 roughly 2.15-2.3 A, i.e. bent but plausible OH...ether bonds; I ordered them by H-bond tightness and by keeping the aldehyde away from the ring/OH. Conformers such as 11, 29, 10, 19, 12, 28, 17 and 27 have only weaker/longer OH...O17 contacts or mostly extended chains, so they are less stabilized but not strongly clashing. The more extended, low-contact structures 20, 9, 30, 26, 16, 18 and 2 are hard to separate; I placed them after the weak-H-bond set because they gain little intramolecular stabilization, but their exact order is uncertain. The bottom group is compact without a compensating H-bond: 1 is only mildly unfavorable, while 6, 24 and especially 23 bring O1 and O9 to about 2.85-2.95 A with H2 not directed at O9, giving lone-pair/dipole repulsion and substituent crowding rather than H-bond stabilization.

The connectivity is an epoxide-bearing glycidyl alcohol with a CH2-NH-CHO side arm. The important donors are the alcohol O1-H2 and amide N12-H16; the important acceptors are epoxide O7 and formamide carbonyl O14. The epoxide bond lengths and the amide cis/trans geometry are essentially conserved, so intrinsic epoxide strain and amide isomerism do not materially separate the conformers. The ranking is therefore driven mainly by intramolecular hydrogen-bond distance and directionality, followed by small-ring closure strain and close polar contacts. 1) Conformers 4 and 30 have the only nearly ideal O-H...O=C interactions: H...O approximately 1.84-1.86 A and O-H...O approximately 149-150 degrees. Both close a favorable six-heavy-atom pseudocycle. Conformer 4 has the slightly shorter contact and is placed first, with 30 essentially tied. 2) Conformers 22 and 29 also form O-H...O=C contacts, but they are longer, about 2.25 and 2.28 A, with donor angles near 128-130 degrees and a less favorable roughly 95-degree C=O...H approach. Conformer 22 is marginally better geometrically. 3) The epoxide-bound group follows. Conformer 16 has a short O-H...O7 contact near 2.00 A and a 120-degree donor angle. Conformer 15 has a somewhat longer but better directed N-H...O7 contact, about 2.19 A and 127 degrees. Alcohol O-H donation makes 16 slightly preferable overall. 4) Conformers 18, 3, and 19 have short O-H...O7 contacts around 2.12-2.17 A but increasingly bent angles, about 115, 115, and 112 degrees. Conformer 19 also has a bent secondary N-H...O1 contact near 2.55 A. 5) Conformers 28 and 17 form comparable five-heavy-atom N-H...O7 closures at about 2.25-2.27 A and roughly 122 degrees; 28 is negligibly shorter, while 17 is slightly less compact. 6) Conformers 20, 12, 7, and 21 have progressively weaker O-H...O7 geometry: approximately 2.24/110, 2.23/110, 2.32/107, and 2.66/106 degrees. The weak secondary N-H...O1 contacts in 20 and 21 are too bent to reverse this trend. 7) Among structures without a clear hydrogen bond, 11 is favored by two bent N-H contacts, about 2.66 A to O1 and 2.77 A to O7. Conformers 24, 8, 26, 1, 2, 9, and 5 possess increasingly weak or poorly aligned N-H...O1 contacts. In 26 the N...O separation near 2.47 A is attractive electrostatically but is also short enough to carry some compression penalty. 8) Conformers 14 and 13 have only very bent N-H...O7 approaches, while 25 has a close N...O separation without useful N-H directionality. Conformers 6, 27, 10, and 23 are mostly neutral, open arrangements with no compensating directed contact; 23 is placed last because it combines the absence of a useful hydrogen bond with poorly oriented alcohol, epoxide, and amide dipoles. There are no severe H-H collisions or obvious epoxide distortions, so the middle and especially the final six positions are uncertain and could interchange under a detailed force-field or quantum calculation.

The atom order implies the same connectivity in every block: a cyclopropanol fragment O1-C2-C3-C4, a flexible linker C3-C7-C9-C10, and a second cyclopropane C10-C11-C12. Because there is only one oxygen and no separate acceptor, intramolecular H-bonding is not a discriminating factor; the dominant terms are cyclopropane/cyclopropane and OH/cyclopropane nonbonded contacts, plus whether the C3-C7-C9-C10 linker is extended or folded. Cyclopropane bond lengths are similar in all conformers, so ring strain is treated as nearly constant and the ranking is driven by through-space separation. I used three geometric diagnostics: C3...C10 end-to-end distance (larger ≈ more extended/less eclipsed linker), distance between the centers of the two cyclopropane rings, and O1...second-ring distance. Conformers 13, 23, 25, 17, 7, 28, 20, 8, 3 and 12 are comparatively extended, with ring centers around 5.0-5.3 Å and the OH group generally pointing away from the second ring; these are placed highest. Within this set, 13/23/25 have the best combination of large ring separation and remote OH, while 28 is very extended but has the oxygen somewhat closer to the distal ring, and 21/27 are extended but show slightly closer O...ring approaches. The folded structures with C3...C10 near 3.05-3.15 Å are penalized, but not equally: 22, 1, 26, 10, 9, 14, 30 and 11 fold the linker while keeping the two ring centroids roughly 4.2-4.7 Å apart and the OH relatively far away, so they are only moderately destabilized. Conformers 4, 6, 15 and 18 are more compact or bring a ring centroid closer to the other ring/OH. The worst geometries are those combining short C3...C10 folding with close ring-ring or OH-ring contacts: 24 and 5 have OH near the distal cyclopropane, 16 and 2 have both compact ring placement and O...ring proximity, 29 is folded with one of the shortest O...ring separations, and 19 has the closest cyclopropane-centroid approach overall, making it the least stable. Uncertainty is largest in the middle of the ranking because subtle torsional eclipsing around C3-C7, C7-C9 and C9-C10 cannot be fully quantified from coordinates alone; the tail is more confidently unfavorable because multiple close contacts coincide.

Step 1 - Skeleton: All 30 blocks share C17H22O5 connectivity.
